The team writes in both Go and Java. New services are in Go 1.23, and the settlement engine and reconciliation batch jobs are Java 21 on Spring Boot, which is roughly 40% of the team's code, so you'd read and change both. For the coding round, it's 60 minutes and you can pick either Go or Java.

[[GIST]] Go and Java, coding round either

I built Skeinrouter at Quillhaven, a Go and Kafka pipeline that replaced a cron job polling carrier integrations every 60 seconds. The main topic has 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID, so ordering stays per shipment, and consumers pause partitions for backpressure instead of dropping events. Outgoing webhooks go through an outbox table in PostgreSQL, and every consumer is idempotent with a dedup table keyed on event ID and carrier ID. That took peak throughput from 9,000 to 41,000 events per second and p99 end-to-end latency from 870 to 140 milliseconds.

[[GIST]] Skeinrouter: 48 partitions, idempotent consumers, outbox

The 48 is right. The topic has 48 partitions. What I said about 24 was the consumer count, not the partition count, and I said it badly. Ordering still holds either way, since the key is the shipment ID and every event for a shipment hashes to one partition.

[[GIST]] 48 partitions, 24 was consumers

I don't have a specific system of mine to walk you through from what's in front of me, so let me be straight about that rather than invent one. What I can do is take you through how I'd design a ledger write path end to end, and where I've done the equivalent work.

The shape I'd start from: every money-moving API takes an idempotency key, and the write goes into a partitioned journal table in Postgres inside a serializable transaction so the double-entry invariants hold. Each service writes an outbox row in the same transaction, and a relay publishes those to Kafka, so the event and the ledger entry can't diverge. Consumers are built to be replayed safely, which is what makes exactly-once in effect possible rather than exactly-once delivery.

Then reconciliation runs as a three-way match between our books, processor reports and bank statements, and the break rate is the number I'd watch. On the operational side, I'd want the pager story clear: what pages, what the runbook says, and how a replay is triggered safely.

If you'd rather go deep on a system I've actually run, tell me which part interests you and I'll take that one.

[[GIST]] ledger write path, idempotency, outbox, reconciliation

The closest thing I've done to money movement is the idempotency work on Skeinrouter: every consumer deduplicated on event ID and carrier ID in PostgreSQL, which took duplicate webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%. That's the same exactly-once-in-effect problem a ledger write path has, and I've also run zero-downtime migrations on PostgreSQL and carried the pager for a tier-1 service.

[[GIST]] idempotency, Postgres, on-call transfer to ledger

The November 2024 incident was a rebalance storm that delayed tracking updates for 3 hours 40 minutes. I don't have the peak consumer lag figure or the timeout setting in front of me, so I'd rather not guess at those. What I can speak to is the fix: we moved all consumer groups to cooperative rebalancing with static membership.

[[GIST]] rebalance storm, 3h40m delay, fix was cooperative rebalancing

48 partitions on tracking.raw, keyed by shipment ID. That key is what gives us per-shipment ordering without any coordination between consumers. We sized it from the projector: one consumer sustains about 1,400 events per second on a single partition, so the peak we planned for needed at least 30, and 48 gave us headroom and divided evenly across both the 12 and 16 pod groups.

[[GIST]] 48 partitions, keyed by shipment ID

An API is the contract one piece of software exposes so another can call it without knowing how it works inside. You agree on the shape of the request and response, and the implementation behind it stays free to change.

Shipment state ended up in **PostgreSQL 15 on RDS**, in the cluster we'd already moved to during Marrowgate, with the shipment_state table hash-partitioned into 32 partitions. The reason was the outbox: the state change and the outgoing webhook row have to commit in one transaction, and a managed key-value store can't give us that. We considered DynamoDB early on, but the outbox requirement killed it, and the shipments in transit fit comfortably on one PostgreSQL primary anyway. The rule we hold to is that shipment-projector is the only writer of shipment state.

[[GIST]] PostgreSQL for transactional outbox

Skeinrouter runs on Amazon MSK, Kafka 3.6, six brokers across three AZs, replication factor three. Three main topics: tracking.raw and tracking.normalized at 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID, and webhook.outbound at 16 keyed by carrier ID, plus a dead-letter topic. I authored the design and built the partitioning and ordering scheme, the shared consumer framework, and the deduplication layer.

[[GIST]] MSK, 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID

The notes don't state a reason for choosing Kafka, so I'll answer from what they do say. What drove it was per-shipment ordering from the partition key with no coordination between consumers, replay so a fixed consumer can reprocess history, and consumer groups scaling by adding pods. We turned down SQS FIFO for its per-group throughput ceiling and no replay, RabbitMQ for no replay and single-consumer ordering, and partitioning by carrier because the largest carrier alone is 9% of traffic and would have made one partition permanently hot.

[[GIST]] ordering, replay, and consumer-group scaling

Offsets are committed only after the database transaction commits, so if a pod dies mid-batch its partitions move to another member of the group and it re-reads from the last committed offset. At most one batch, up to 500 records, gets processed again, and the deduplication table turns those repeats into no-ops. So nothing is lost and nothing is applied twice.

[[GIST]] re-read from last committed offset, deduped

The worst one was a consumer-lag incident on Skeinrouter, our tracking pipeline at Quillhaven, in November 2024. We were mid-rollout, 720 carriers already live, and a routine rolling restart of the 16 projector pods kicked off a rebalance storm. The group was still on eager rebalancing, so every pod restart stopped the whole group, and while the database absorbed the backlog a batch could run past the 30-second max.poll.interval, members got evicted for being slow, and each eviction triggered another rebalance.

I took incident command at 14:20, we raised it to Sev-1 at 15:30 with lag peaking at 96 million events and the worst shipments 47 minutes behind. We paused the deploy, scaled the group down to 8 pods and raised max.poll.interval to 5 minutes, which stabilised it, and the backlog drained by 17:45. Three hours forty total, no events lost, nothing rolled back, because the deduplication table kept the replays out. The follow-up was moving every consumer group to cooperative rebalancing with static membership, one-pod-at-a-time restarts behind a lag gate, and a burn-rate alert on consumer lag.

[[GIST]] rebalance storm, 3h40 lag, fixed with cooperative rebalancing

At 500 to 1, that's 60 billion redirects a month, so about 23,000 reads per second average. With the brief's 4x peak, I'd size the redirect path for roughly 92,000 reads per second at peak.

Straight answer: the outbox part is a close match, the idempotency-keys-on-write-APIs part is not.

On the outbox, Skeinrouter has exactly that shape. The shipment-projector writes the state change and the outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction, and outbox-relay reads it with SKIP LOCKED and publishes. That's the pattern the JD is describing, and I built and reviewed it.

On idempotency, what I built is idempotent consumers, not idempotency keys on write endpoints. The deduplication table is keyed on event ID and carrier ID, so a replayed Kafka event becomes a no-op. That's consumer-side dedup. The JD is asking for the other half: a client-supplied key on every write API so a retried POST doesn't create a second record. I haven't built that, and I'd say so rather than blur the two.

The honest framing is that I've done the replay-safety and outbox side in production, and I understand the write-path key side well enough to design it, but I haven't shipped it. Also worth flagging: Skeinrouter is freight tracking, not money movement, so the correctness bar is real but it isn't a ledger.

[[GIST]] outbox yes, write-API idempotency keys no

The bug is that `tiered_cost` treats `upper` as the size of each tier instead of the cumulative boundary. It should subtract the previous tier's upper bound, so the second tier covers units 1,001 to 10,000, not another 10,000.

[[CALC]]
units = 12000
tier1 = 1000 * 50 = 50000
tier2 = (10000 - 1000) * 30 = 9000 * 30 = 270000
tier3 = (12000 - 10000) * 10 = 2000 * 10 = 20000
total = 50000 + 270000 + 20000 = 340000
[[/CALC]]

For 12,000 units it should return **340,000 mills**: 1,000 at 50, 9,000 at 30, and 2,000 at 10. The current code returns 590,000 because it charges 10,000 units in the middle tier.

[[GIST]] cumulative bounds, not tier sizes

Yes, that's a real race. TryConsume reads the counter under a read lock, releases it, then writes under a write lock, so two goroutines for the same tenant can both read the same value and both pass the check. The fix is to do the read, the check and the increment in one write lock, or use a per-tenant atomic.

I've hit this shape of bug for real. On Skeinrouter I made every consumer idempotent with a deduplication table in PostgreSQL keyed on event ID and carrier ID, which cut duplicate status webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%.

[[GIST]] check-then-act race, fix under one lock

Time is O(n), each character visited at most once, and space is O(1). And yes, this already avoids a second string. I never build a filtered copy, I just move the two pointers past non-alphanumeric characters in place and compare lowercased characters directly.

[[GIST]] O(n) time, O(1) space, no copy

## Approach
Two pointers, one from each end, skipping anything that isn't a letter or digit and comparing lowercased characters. That gives linear time and constant extra space, which is what the sheet asks for. I'll use `str.isalnum()` and `str.lower()` rather than building a filtered copy, so I never allocate a second string.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

## Complexity
Time O(n), each character is visited at most once by the two pointers. Space O(1), only the two index variables, no filtered copy.

[[GIST]] two pointers, skip non-alnum, O(1) space

I'm primary on-call for the dispatch domain one week in five, and I've been incident commander on 9 Sev-1 and Sev-2 incidents since April 2024. The load's come down a lot: we took Sev-1s in the dispatch domain from 14 in 2023 to 5 in 2025, and median time to restore from 52 minutes to 19.

[[GIST]] on-call one week in five, load falling

I start from the user journey, not the infrastructure. For a new service I'd ask what the caller actually experiences, pick the one or two signals that track that, and set the target from what we can already measure rather than a round number. Then I'd check the error budget is realistic for the team, wire burn-rate alerts instead of threshold alerts, and revisit it after a few weeks of real traffic.

The first step, the clinic page and service list, is server-rendered so the largest element is already in the HTML, and clinic profile data uses incremental static regeneration with a 300-second revalidation. Slots are fetched in the browser and never cached longer than 30 seconds, because a stale slot is a double booking. The five steps are client-side transitions with route-level code splitting, each prefetched while the owner fills in the one before.

We did try keeping the SPA and only splitting the bundle. The prototype got mobile LCP to 3.1 seconds and no further, so that was rejected.

[[GIST]] server-render first step, client-fetch slots

The one that still stings is the March 2023 regression on Fernlatch, the booking flow rebuild I tech led. Release 0.19 formatted slot times during server rendering, so the server formatted them in its own time zone and the browser formatted them again in the clinic's. Where the two differed, the markup didn't match, React threw away the server-rendered tree and re-rendered in the browser, and for clinics outside the server's zone the first paint showed slots an hour off. A support ticket from a clinic in the Azores and a real-user-monitoring alert landed within minutes of each other the next evening, we rolled back 25 minutes after detection, and the fix went out the following Monday. In the 26 hours it was live, 312 bookings were made at the wrong hour, and p75 interaction delay went from 130 ms to 410 ms. Support contacted every affected clinic and owner within two days. The fix sends slots as ISO strings with the clinic's time zone and formats them only in the browser after mount. What I changed afterwards was the process: a Playwright run in three time zones, and a rule that any hydration error fails the build. If I did it again I'd have that multi-time-zone run in place before the first server-rendered release, not after.

[[GIST]] time-zone hydration bug, 312 wrong bookings, tz CI

On Fernlatch, the booking flow, I was tech lead of three frontend engineers with one designer, from September 2022 to April 2023. We rebuilt it in React and TypeScript with server rendering on Next.js, route-level code splitting, and image sizing at build time. Mobile p75 LCP went from 4.3 seconds to 1.7, interaction delay from 380 to 120 milliseconds, and first-load JavaScript from 1.9 MB to 610 kB. Booking completion rose from 61.2% to 66.8% in a six-week A/B experiment, and almost all of that gain came from phones. On your 350 kB budget, I'd want to know what's in your baseline before I say how close that is.

[[GIST]] Fernlatch: 610 kB, LCP 1.7s, +5.6pt completion

The brief gives me the vendor limit, so I can do the arithmetic. SMS is 5% of 180 million a day, which is 9 million SMS a day. Average is 9,000,000 / 86,400, so about 104 per second. Peak is 6 times average, so roughly 625 SMS per second. The vendor caps at 500 per second, so yes, peak exceeds the cap and I need a buffer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    api["Send API"] -->|"enqueue"| queue["SMS Queue"]
    queue --> worker["SMS Worker"]
    worker -->|"rate-limited 500/s"| vendor["SMS Vendor"]
    worker -->|"record attempt"| log[("Delivery Log")]
    worker -->|"failed, attempts left"| retry["Retry Queue with backoff"]
    retry --> worker
    worker -->|"attempts exhausted"| dlq["Dead-Letter Queue"]
```

The send API only enqueues, so it stays inside the 2 second p99 for transactional messages. A worker drains the queue at the vendor's 500 per second, which smooths the burst instead of dropping it. The excess at peak is about 125 per second, so a short burst drains in seconds and the queue absorbs it. The tradeoff is added latency for promotional SMS, which is fine since those have a 15 minute budget, but transactional SMS still needs priority so codes and alerts don't sit behind a campaign. On failure, retries go back through a delayed queue with a dedup key, and anything out of attempts lands in the dead-letter queue.

[[GIST]] peak 625/s vs 500/s cap, buffer needed

The problem is the N+1: one query for the members, then two more per member inside the loop, so a 250-person team is 1 + 250×2 = **501 round trips**.

The fix is to batch it: one query for members, then one grouped query for task counts and one for last logins, keyed by member id. That's **3 round trips** total, regardless of team size.

I haven't built a production event pipeline myself, so I don't want to invent topics and throughput numbers I can't stand behind. What I can do is walk through how I'd design one, and where the real decisions are.

The core choices are partitioning key, delivery semantics, and consumer model. I'd partition by the entity that needs ordering, say user ID or order ID, so all events for one entity land on the same partition and stay ordered, while spreading load across partitions. Topic count follows the number of independent streams and retention needs, not the number of consumers.

For throughput, the ceiling is usually per-partition write rate times partition count, so I'd size partitions from peak events per second with headroom, then measure consumer lag rather than guess. I'd start with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, since exactly-once is expensive and rarely worth it unless duplicates actually break something.

[[GIST]] partition by entity, size from peak, measure lag
